historical_timeline.summary: Arrived at Scutari with a party of thirty-eight nurses.
Fell dangerously ill with Crimean fever at Balaclava.
Returned to England and pressed for a royal commission on army health.
Overworked and ill during the commission; rest at Malvern; took to her bed or couch but kept working.
Completed her 830-page statistical report on army health; elected to the Statistical Society.
Further severe episode; unable to walk, with what was described as spondylitis.
First woman appointed to the Order of Merit; by then she rarely left her room.
Died in her sleep at 10 South Street, London, aged 90.

claims.statement: Florence Nightingale was born on May 12, 1820, in Florence, Italy, where her parents were on a European tour; her elder sister, Frances Parthenope, was born in 1819.
In October 1854 she led a party of thirty-eight nurses from London to the British military hospitals at Scutari, arriving in November 1854.

In May 1855, a few days after crossing to Balaclava to inspect the hospitals in the Crimea, she fell ill with what the army doctors called Crimean fever. She was carried to the Castle Hospital, was dangerously ill and, by her own later account, very near to death; she was reported out of danger on May 24 and made a slow and painful recovery before returning to work at Scutari.
claims.clinical_interpretation: Contemporary label; no laboratory diagnosis was possible. She herself called it typhus.

source_links.locator: Volume 1, chapter on the Crimea: the attack of Crimean fever

claims.statement: Modern writers have interpreted her Crimean fever as brucellosis and her long later illness as chronic brucellosis.
claims.clinical_interpretation: Retrospective interpretation without laboratory confirmation. The 1998 review argues that 32 years of illness fit chronic brucellosis; the biography of record calls the fever probably brucellosis, citing the 1995 BMJ analysis. Used only as context; it is not a diagnosis in the historical record.

source_links.locator: Calls the fever probably Brucella infection, citing the 1995 BMJ article

claims.statement: She returned to England in the summer of 1856, emaciated and tense, and pressed for a royal commission on the health of the army, which was established in 1857.
claims.clinical_interpretation: The biography of record gives July 1856 for her return; the National Army Museum gives August 1856.

claims.statement: In 1857, while working on her report for the commission, she was overworking and in failing health; she sought rest at Malvern in August and September and again in December, but would not stop working. She collapsed with cardiac symptoms so severe that it was thought she would die, and afterward suffered from nausea, insomnia, and palpitations. On her doctors' orders she took to her bed or couch but continued to work, the beginning of about twenty years of invalidism.
claims.clinical_interpretation: Contemporary descriptions. The biography of record suggests the collapse was probably a sequel of the Crimean fever; that link is interpretation, not documented diagnosis.

source_links.locator: Volume 1, chapter covering November 1856 to August 1857: Malvern in August, September, and December

claims.statement: Her own 830-page report, Notes on Matters Affecting the Health, Efficiency, and Hospital Administration of the British Army (1858), used statistical evidence to show how much army mortality was due to conditions in the hospitals. She was elected to the Statistical Society, the first woman member.
claims.clinical_interpretation: The biography of record dates her election to 1858; the National Army Museum gives 1859.

claims.statement: Although often confined to her bed or her room for decades, she directed reform largely by correspondence, writing some 13,000 letters and publishing more than 200 books, reports, and pamphlets on hospital planning and organization.
claims.clinical_interpretation: Her working life from bed is documented and is part of the teaching point.

claims.statement: In 1861 she had a further severe episode in which she was unable to walk and suffered what her biographers describe as alarming spondylitis.
claims.clinical_interpretation: The basis of the spondylitis label is not recorded; it is sometimes cited as a feature of chronic brucellosis, which remains an interpretation.

claims.statement: Her prolonged illness has also been read retrospectively as what is now called myalgic encephalomyelitis/chronic fatigue syndrome, while other writers have proposed neurasthenia, a psychosomatic illness, or illness used to secure time for work.
claims.clinical_interpretation: Competing retrospective readings with no agreement; none is a documented diagnosis.

source_links.locator: States she later suffered from what is now known as chronic fatigue syndrome
Notes the psychosomatic theory among diagnoses proposed for her invalidism

claims.statement: She spent almost the whole of her last fifteen years in her room in South Street, London; her eyesight was failing by the late 1880s, and from 1902 she could write only with great difficulty. In 1907 she became the first woman appointed to the Order of Merit.
She died in her sleep in her room at 10 South Street, Park Lane, London, on August 13, 1910, aged 90.
claims.clinical_interpretation: One medical historian gives old age and heart failure as the cause; no death certificate was reviewed.

synthetic_episode.teaching_objective: Recognize post-infectious myalgic encephalomyelitis/chronic fatigue syndrome in a 37-year-old nurse administrator and statistician, make the diagnosis by clinical criteria after a focused set of exclusion tests (including a reasoned decision about past brucellosis), and manage it by NICE NG206 and CDC guidance: energy management and pacing without graded exercise therapy, orthostatic intolerance measures, sleep and pain care, mood screening, function scales, and workplace adjustments that protect the productive working life that matters most to her.

hpi.narrative: Ms. Nightingale returns two weeks after her first visit to review her tests, and saw the infectious diseases physician this morning. She has kept the activity and symptom diary we agreed on. It shows the pattern she described: on days she works more than about three hours or goes out, she feels worse the next day or the day after, with aches as if she had the flu, heavier fatigue, and poor concentration that take two to four days to settle. She sleeps nine hours but wakes unrefreshed. Standing at the stove or in a line still makes her lightheaded with a pounding heart within a few minutes. She has started drinking more fluid, about 1.8 L a day. She takes acetaminophen two or three times a week for muscle aches and headache. Her mood is frustrated but not low, and she has no thoughts of self-harm.

assessment_plan.display: Myalgic encephalomyelitis/chronic fatigue syndrome, post-infectious, moderate
assessment_plan.assessment: She meets the NICE criteria (debilitating fatigue worsened by activity, post-exertional malaise, unrefreshing sleep, and cognitive difficulty for well over three months) and the IOM criteria, with orthostatic intolerance on the standing test (heart rate rise of 26/min without hypotension). The exclusion tests are normal apart from a low vitamin D, and the infectious diseases physician finds no evidence of relapsed or focal brucellosis. A PHQ-9 of 8 reflects the physical items of the illness, not depression
plan: Diagnosis explained: a real, recognized illness with no diagnostic test; written care and support plan given, including a flare plan

Energy management: keep the diary, set a baseline below the level that triggers post-exertional malaise, plan rest before and between tasks, and break work into blocks of about 30 minutes; first session with the clinic occupational therapist next week
No graded exercise therapy and no advice to push through or exercise more
Orthostatic intolerance: raise fluids to 2 to 2.5 L a day, add salt with meals (blood pressure 106/68 mmHg), use waist-high compression garments, and do tasks seated or reclined
Sleep: a regular sleep window; keep daytime rests to short periods lying down
Pain: continue acetaminophen as needed; avoid opioids and sedatives
Work: a letter to her employer supporting home working, a reclined workstation, and flexible hours

assessment_plan.assessment: Infectious diseases consultation today: no clinical or laboratory sign of relapse or focal infection (no fever, normal ESR and CRP, no spinal or joint findings). Repeat serology would not help
plan: No further antibiotics or serology
Call for fever, night sweats, or new back or joint pain

assessment_plan.assessment: 25-hydroxyvitamin D 17 ng/mL; she is indoors most days
plan: Start cholecalciferol 2,000 units daily
Recheck 25-hydroxyvitamin D in about three months

hpi.narrative: Ms. Nightingale is a 38-year-old woman with post-infectious ME/CFS, managed with energy management since March, and a past brucellosis treated abroad, who asked for a same-day visit. Three days ago she developed a sore throat and runny nose, followed by a dry cough. A colleague who visited to work with her had a cold last week. Two home COVID-19 antigen tests, two days apart, were negative. Her highest home temperature was 37.8 °C. Since yesterday her fatigue, muscle aches, and brain fog have been much worse than her usual day-to-day variation, and she has spent most of both days in bed. She has already started her written flare plan: she cancelled her meetings, cut her work to short reading periods, and is resting in a darkened room. She is drinking about 2 L a day and taking acetaminophen 1 g twice a day, which helps the sore throat and aches. She has no night sweats, back or joint pain, or other symptoms resembling those of her illness abroad, and she wanted to be sure this is not that infection returning.

referral.question: Suspected post-infectious ME/CFS in a 37-year-old nurse administrator who was treated for brucellosis abroad. Before we attribute her symptoms to ME/CFS, please assess for relapsed or focal brucellosis or another persisting infection
referral.pertinent_history: Nearly three years ago, while leading nurses at an overseas field hospital, she had a severe febrile illness with sweats and aches; a Brucella agglutination titer there was reported positive and she completed six weeks of doxycycline and rifampin, with the fever resolving. Since then she has had debilitating fatigue worsened by activity, post-exertional malaise lasting days, unrefreshing sleep, and cognitive difficulty, worse after an intense period of work last year. She is housebound most days. Today she is afebrile; a ten-minute standing test shows a heart rate rise of 26/min without hypotension. No spinal or joint tenderness and no liver or spleen enlargement. The NICE exclusion tests, including ESR and CRP, were drawn today
questions: Is there any clinical or laboratory evidence of relapsed brucellosis or a focal complication such as spondylitis, sacroiliitis, or endocarditis?
Would repeat Brucella serology or blood cultures help now?
Is any other infection related to her field-hospital work worth excluding?
Is there any role for further antibiotics?

consultant_note.history: Ms. Nightingale is seen at the request of Dr. Marchetti. Nearly three years ago, on an overseas field-hospital deployment, she had several weeks of high fever, drenching sweats, and generalized aches; a Brucella agglutination titer was reported positive, and she completed six weeks of doxycycline with rifampin. The fever never returned. She has had no night sweats, weight loss, localized back or hip pain, or joint swelling since, and no unpasteurized dairy since returning. What persists is fatigue worsened by activity with delayed post-exertional malaise, unrefreshing sleep, cognitive difficulty, and lightheadedness on standing. Occupational tuberculosis screening on her return was negative, and she reports no needle-stick injuries

assessment.assessment: No evidence of relapse or a focal complication. Relapses usually come within months of treatment and present with fever, which she has not had; she has no spinal or sacroiliac findings, no murmur, no organ enlargement, and normal inflammatory markers and blood count

Brucella agglutinating antibodies can stay positive for a long time after successful treatment, so a repeat titer cannot separate past from active infection and would only cause confusion. Blood cultures are useful only if fever returns

Nothing in her exposures calls for further infection testing now. The one-time HIV, hepatitis B, and hepatitis C screening recommended for all adults is reasonable to complete with her preventive care
Her course fits a post-infectious fatigue syndrome after brucellosis rather than ongoing infection. Prolonged or repeated antibiotics do not help post-infectious fatigue and carry real harms
